summary: ⁠One Sol to Rescue is a bilingual browser game that lets children ages 7–12 run a damaged Mars outpost. Players help Mark and his robot Beep survive 30 Martian days by sharing limited power between life support, heating, food production, communications, and repairs. During a dust storm, for example, players can protect the solar panels by folding them, but lose heat that night. The game uses real solar flare dates and classes from NASA’s DONKI archive and simulates their effects on the outpost. A final debrief connects decisions to their consequences and links to the NASA record used in the mission. The game runs in English and Russian, online or offline from a single HTML file.
details:
One Sol to Rescue makes the trade-offs of running a Mars outpost playable for young learners. Each sol, players check their oxygen, food, and available power, decide which systems to run, and plan work within limits on time and spare parts. They can inspect damaged equipment, decide whether to clean or repair it, and prepare for evacuation. During a solar flare, taking shelter limits modeled radiation exposure but pauses greenhouse work and repairs for that sol. Players can review daily results, and the final debrief traces important gains and losses back to earlier choices.

⁠We built the game with JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. Three.js renders the 3D outpost and orbital views, with an SVG fallback for devices without hardware WebGL 2. Node.js and esbuild bundle the game and its assets into a single HTML file. We use Playwright and GitHub Actions to check browser behavior and the offline build. The embedded NASA DONKI archive supplies real flare dates and classes. Radiation risk, crop growth, and resource consumption use simplified game rules.

⁠We designed the controls and Beep’s guidance so players can start with one system and learn the others as they play. Presentation Mode lets a teacher or judge replay a short scenario and discuss the cost of different choices. English and Russian support, offline play, and teacher prompts make the game easier to use in a classroom. Our next step is to test whether students can predict and explain the consequences of their decisions.


⁠Source code: https://github.com/Xasoek/qanatHub-game
